Issued at 123 PM EDT Wed Oct 7 2026

*** WARM AND DRY INTO SATURDAY ***

Early Wednesday afternoon, west-northwest flow aloft was present 
over the local area between a ridge across the Great Plains and 
upper level trough over the Great Lakes. Like yesterday, deep mixing 
will add a couple more degrees to surface temperatures for highs in 
the upper 70s (east) to low 80s (west), though it'll still feel mild 
for most - especially in the shade - as low relative humidity keeps 
apparent, or "feels like," temperatures a couple degrees below 
actual air temperatures.

A decaying cool front will sink south and wash out over southern 
Indiana tonight, while in its wake surface high pressure will shift 
east from the Midwest to the Appalachians tomorrow into Friday. This 
will result in gentle northeast winds which will keep the airmass 
dry and perhaps 1-2 degrees less warm during the day tomorrow. In 
addition, if we lose the wind overnight into Friday morning, rural 
low-lying areas may once again dip into the upper 30s or at least 
low 40s - though the probability of widespread frost is very low 
(less than 2%).

Meanwhile, tropical storm Isaias will be brewing over the Gulf,
and on Friday it should start to lift northwards towards the 
coast as it merges with a cutoff low over Texas/Louisiana. In 
response, the local area will see strengthening easterly flow 
Friday into Saturday, by which time some guidance shows a 
notable downsloping effect in the pressure gradient field off of
the Appalachians. While this would have a drying effect, the 
abundant tropical moisture accompanying Isaias' remnants may 
offset this - though perhaps not until late Saturday, sparking 
at least low concerns over fire weather early in the day. While 
confidence is much higher in daytime RH values of 20-30% 
(locally lower) on Friday, winds should be light enough (gusts 
generally less than 15 mph) to minimize any fire weather 
concerns despite minimum afternoon 10-hour fuel moistures of 
7-9%. All the while, the continued dry and seasonably warm 
weather will result in expanding and worsening drought 
conditions.

*** TROPICAL REMNANTS TO BRING BENEFICIAL RAIN(?) BY SUNDAY ***

As what's left of Isaias lifts toward the local area, strong 
diffluence and synoptic lift in the right entrance region of the 
trough should lead to an expansive rain shield which models suggest 
will likely (80% chance) enter the local area sometime between early 
Saturday afternoon (LREF 10th percentile onset time) and around dawn 
Sunday morning (LREF 90th percentile onset time). The overnight 
Saturday night into Sunday morning timing (given by the LREF mean) 
of the heaviest bands of precipitation associated with the tropical 
remnants suggests diurnally-driven instability will be very low - 
limiting the risk for tornadoes. However, the screaming wind fields 
accompanying this system raise concerns about locally strong winds 
should any heavier showers/storms mix them down to the surface. In 
addition, the strong directional wind shear on the east side of the 
surface low - which the National Hurricane Center (NCH) suggests 
will track near or west of the local area - suggests that should its 
northward trek speed up, we'll have to watch southern Kentucky for 
brief spin ups as GFS soundings show strongly curved hodographs 
featuring 500-1000 m^2/s^2 0-3km SRH Saturday evening. Fortunately, 
the global models, whose resolution is too coarse to capture 
convective features, suggest gradient winds associated with this 
system are unlikely to be problematic with EPS (European ensemble) 
mean peak gusts around 20-30 mph Saturday night into Sunday; it 
wouldn't be surprising to see this increase, knowing how models 
struggle to resolve tropical systems, so we'll keep a close eye on 
it as we get closer to the weekend.

The main story with this system will be the rainfall, though amounts 
remain a source of considerable uncertainty with National Blend of 
Models (NBM) 25th-75th percentile 48-hour rainfall totals through 
8am Monday morning ranging from roughly 0.75 to 2.25 inches across 
the local area. This means that, at any given location, the chance 
of total rain amounts falling either inside or outside of this range 
is 50% - that's a lot of spread. Given the antecedent dry 
conditions, RFC 6-hour Flash Flood Guidance (FFG) - or the minimum 
amount of rainfall required to induce flooding - is running 3.5-4.5 
inches, which is around NBM's ensemble max for the whole event. This 
would indicate our flooding risk is low, though not negligible, 
since the global models comprising NBM won't resolve convective 
processes which could enhance rainfall rates; any flooding would 
likely be confined to a localized band of heavier rain - fueled by a 
60-75 kt 850mb LLJ Saturday night.
